children: The Federal Reserve’s “higher for longer” stance is not landing evenly across corporate credit.

Apollo's chief economist Torsten Slok argues the pressure is concentrated at the bottom of the ratings stack: CCC borrowers, many of them from the 2021–22 cheap-money vintage, are now colliding with a refinancing wall while cash available to service debt is shrinking.

CCC yields near 15%, making that reset expensive. The stress is most visible in private-equity-backed technology, healthcare, and consumer discretionary issuers—businesses that combine floating-rate debt, thin margins, and rising disruption risk, including from AI. Those names have little room to absorb years of elevated coupons.

Policy transmission is lagging and uneven. Investment-grade and stronger high-yield issuers locked in cheap fixed-rate debt have felt little of the tightening cycle. The most leveraged borrowers feel all of it as rates reset and maturities roll. The bill from the zero-rate era is arriving first on the weakest balance sheets.

For allocators, the implication is quality, not yield-chasing. Higher-rated credit still offers attractive all-in yields without the default, restructuring, and liability-management risk now clustered in the CCC sleeve. Companies that generate earnings can pay the higher cost of capital. Many that cannot are already being forced to confront it.

title: Higher-for-longer is squeezing the weakest credits first, Apollo notes
